newsitem.title: UK: British author Laurie Lee dies at 82.
newsitem.headline: British author Laurie Lee dies at 82.

text.p: Laurie Lee, who immortalised a sensual and earthy way of English country living in his classic novel "Cider with Rosie", died on Wednesday, his publisher said.
Lee was 82 and died at his home in Gloucestershire, western England.
In March, Lee went into hospital for abdominal surgery, having grown increasingly frail in recent years.
But his mind remained sharp and his voice mellifluous. And Lee's books are still compulsory reading for schoolchildren across Britain, with their warm evocation of a long-lost way of life.
"Cider With Rosie", an autobiographical classic that sold more than six million copies, was published in 1959.
It changed Lee's life.

"My wife Cathie and I had been living on buckets of spaghetti and burning the furniture in the winter until then," Lee recalled of his first and best-known book in which a village girl, Rosie, "baptized (him) with her cidrous kisses".
Until fame hit, Lee had been just another struggling poet and his publisher was so parsimonious that Lee had to write his own publicity blurb on the cover.
"I wrote that Cider With Rosie was likely to become a classic," said Lee.
It was one of 12 novels on top of five books of award-winning poetry.

"As I Walked Out One Midsummer Morning" described how Lee left home aged 19 with only a blanket and a violin. He travelled to Spain on a one-way ticket, finding a mediaeval world that fired his imagination.

In 1991 he published the final volume of an acclaimed trilogy "Moment of War", which relives the horror of the Spanish Civil War in which he enrolled as a volunteer on the anti-fascist Republican side.
But his love affair with Spain never matched his deep-seated passion for the sensual pleasures of rural Britain.
"There's nothing more glorious than tickling a girl under a haystack when you're not taking love that seriously," he wrote.
Born on June 26, 1914, Lee was brought up by his mother and three older half-sisters. He married Catherine, 17 years his junior, in 1950 and had one daughter, Jessy, now in her 30s.
For an ageing Lee, Jessy was a gift: "a late fall into my life, lying purple and dented like a little bruised plum."
He spent his last years in the village of Slad where he was born, campaigning against the developers who dared invade his idyll. Life had moved on and sped up since Lee was a boy.
"The speed limit and rhythm of our day was eight miles an hour -- no cars, just horses," he said in a recent interview.
Eight people were crammed together in one cottage, so Lee -- a sickly child and an introvert -- escaped to the peace of a yew tree to scribble down his adventures.
"I couldn't get a word in edgeways at home. We were like birds in a nest trampling on each other's fantasies."
Lee said he was lucky to have lived so long, seen so much.

"I have unbounded gratitude at having known this world," he recalled in his later years. "Through all its disorders and tragedies, being down on this earth is a unique experience and all I'm writing is an attempt to explain it."
